hero.subtitle: Your guide through the landscape of archaeological data
hero.description1: From excavations, surveys, and watching briefs, we collect and manage archaeological data from all over the Czech Republic, ensuring it remains openly accessible in a digital form.
hero.description2: The AMCR is developed with a wide range of users in mind. We have tailored the design and features of each tool to suit the needs of a diverse audience, including professional and amateur archaeologists, state administration, and the general public.

quickApps.app2.subtitle: AMCR >
quickApps.app2.expandedText:
The Archaeological Map of the Czech Republic is a powerful tool for the central registration and long-term preservation of archaeological records in the Czech Republic.

Register and deposit your fieldwork data with ease – manage projects, events, and documentation in one place using the trusted digital repository AMCR.

On top of that, we ensure that your data remains accessible for future generations!

The virtual research room is open to you 24/7.

tools.label: Tools
tools.title: The Archaeological Map of the Czech Republic and its tools in a nutshell
tools.sectionTitle: The Archaeological Map of the Czech Republic and its tools in a nutshell
tools.tool1.title: Archaeological Map of the Czech Republic (AMCR)
tools.tool1.description: A core information system for recording archaeological fieldwork and related activities in the Czech Republic. It allows users to report groundworks, deposit data on the course and outcomes of excavations and surveys, and serves as a trusted digital repository for archaeological documentation. The system also provides data for other AIS CR tools.
tools.tool2.title: Digital Archive of the AMCR
tools.tool2.description: A web application for browsing and downloading data (such as documents) archived in the AMCR, offering access to information on excavations, sites, and finds collected in the archives of the Archaeological Institutes of the Czech Academy of Sciences in Brno and Prague.
tools.tool3.title: Map of Archaeological Organisations (OAO Map)
tools.tool3.description: A map that provides an overview of organisations authorised to conduct archaeological excavations in the Czech Republic, along with the exact geographical scope of their remit. You can quickly identify who holds the authorisation, where they operate, and how to contact them, making it easy to get in touch with archaeologists to arrange a new excavation or start a collaborative project.
tools.tool4.title: Portal of Amateur Collaborators and the Register of Individual Finds (AMCR-PAS)
tools.tool4.description: A portal for reporting and publishing archaeological finds resulting from partnerships between archaeological organisations and amateur collaborators. It also establishes a formal framework for such active collaboration within the bounds of the State Monument Care Act.
tools.tool5.title: 3D Library
tools.tool5.description: A tool for cataloguing archaeological 3D models and textures, forming one of the modules of the AMCR and the Digital Archive.
tools.tool6.title: AMCR API
tools.tool6.description: A set of application programming interfaces enabling automated extraction of data from the AMCR. It consists of an OAI-PMH API for accessing all metadata, a file API for downloading data, and an authentication API that can be used either independently (authorisation and authentication via an AMCR user account) or as part of authorised access to the OAI-PMH and file API.
tools.tool7.title: AMCR Knowledge Base
tools.tool7.description: The AMCR Knowledge Base provides detailed guides on how to use each module of the AMCR, explains the data model and overall system architecture, and summarises its history. It also includes the AMCR Newsletter – a non-periodical circular for users, which explains specific updates in detail and places them in the context of heritage management in the Czech Republic.
additionalServices.title: The AIS CR infrastructure
additionalServices.description: The Archaeological Map of the Czech Republic is the heart of the large research infrastructure, the Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic (AIS CR). The AIS CR offers a wide range of tools and services for both the research community and the general public.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: How can I report a new construction project?
faq.a1: Notification of a construction or other project planned in an area with archaeological finds (anywhere in the Czech Republic except for surface mines and quarries), in accordance with Section 22(2) of Act No. 20/1987 Coll., on State Monument Care, can be submitted via an online form.
faq.q2: How can I find an archaeological organisation authorised to carry out excavations in a specific location in the Czech Republic?
faq.a2: You can find an overview of more than 100 authorised archaeological organisations, including the geographical scope of their remit and contact information, in the Map of Archaeological Organisations application.
faq.q3: How can I take part in archaeological fieldwork?
faq.a3: In the Czech Republic, it is not permitted to search for and recover archaeological finds without legal authorisation. If you are interested in joining the network of amateur collaborators working with archaeological organisations and participating in surface surveys, please read the collaboration guidelines here.
faq.q4: I am having trouble using the AMCR. What should I do, and where can I find information?
faq.a4:
An extensive knowledge base is available for the AMCR, offering detailed guides, explaining how the system works, and summarising its history. It also contains the AMCR Newsletter with additional information and a section with methodological guidelines. We recommend consulting these resources first.

If you still need help, please contact us at amcr@arup.cas.cz (support for Bohemia) or amcr@arub.cz (support for Moravia and Silesia), and we will be happy to assist you.
faq.q5: What should I do if the AMCR is not working properly or I get an error message?
faq.a5: A list of the most common error messages and recommended solutions can be found here. In many cases, your feedback helps us detect and fix issues in time. If you encounter a specific problem, please contact us at amcr@arup.cas.cz (support for Bohemia) or amcr@arub.cz (support for Moravia and Silesia).
faq.q6: Why should I sign up and create a user account in the AMCR, and how can I do it?
faq.a6: While you can view most basic data in the Digital Archive of the AMCR without restrictions, viewing or downloading attached documents is usually not possible, and some record details may be hidden. You also will not have access to features that make browsing easier, such as saving favourites or storing certain user settings automatically. Without registration, you cannot add any data to the AMCR, except for reporting construction project or other ground disturbances. If you are an archaeologist or require a higher level of access for other reasons, we cannot grant it to you without a user account. Having an account also allows you to receive the AMCR Newsletter with the latest updates. Signing up is simple and can be done here.
faq.q7: How open is the AMCR data? What can I do with it, and how should I cite it?
faq.a7:
Data archived in the AMCR is published in the Digital Archive virtual research room and available with differing levels of information, depending on the user account. Our approach follows the principle 'as open as possible, as restricted as necessary'. Detailed information on data openness can be found here. Options for accessing data via API are described here and here.

Documents uploaded to the AMCR are usually made available under the rules agreed in licence agreements with individual data providers. Documents uploaded by archaeologists from authorised organisations are generally subject to a three-year protected period (embargo). After this time, they become available to users with 'Researcher' access or higher, which is granted upon signing up and creating an account.

Most AMCR data are published under the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International (CC BY-NC 4.0) licence. Detailed instructions on using and citing data are provided here.
faq.q8: What are the main types of archaeological projects, and how should I record them?
faq.a8: For recording purposes, the archaeological institutes distinguish three types of archaeological research projects: rescue projects, research projects, and minimally invasive surveys. The definitions of these terms, in the context of both the State Monument Care Act and the AMCR, are given in one of the methodological guidelines. Rescue excavations are typically managed according to the standard AMCR practice. The process for research projects is specified separately due to the requirement for prior consent. The administration of survey projects should follow the guidelines for the AMCR-PAS.
faq.q9: How should I add a record retrospectively for older fieldwork, a record for large-scale excavation covering extensive areas, or other specific cases?
faq.a9:
For retrospective recording of older excavations, we recommend using the Individual Events module. For large-scale excavations, however, we suggest creating a project and recording sub-activities for individual fieldwork stages (e.g. distinguished by cadastral areas or other logical units), enabling better navigation in the data and ensuring an appropriate level of metadata detail. This approach can also be used for surface surveys and other activities where, rather than creating a joint project, it is more practical to record individual events for each particular surveyed area (one continuous area per event).

For these specific cases, we strongly recommend consulting the AMCR administrators in advance to make sure the information is recorded in the right way: amcr@arup.cas.cz (support for Bohemia) or amcr@arub.cz (support for Moravia and Silesia).
faq.q10: What should a fieldwork report look like? What should it contain, and are there variations?
faq.a10:
The content requirements for a fieldwork report are outlined in the methodological guidelines in our knowledge base. In some cases, it is possible to submit a simplified version, especially if the excavation yielded only artefacts without further context or the archaeological finding is of a very small scale.

A fieldwork report does not have to be a single document. In the AMCR, multiple files in various formats can be attached to a Document record. The most common format is PDF, but if you have an inventory list of finds, contexts, deposits, samples, etc., prepared in a spreadsheet, it is better to attach it in XLSX or CSV format. Other accepted formats include TXT, TIFF, PNG, JPG, and SVG. Submitting a fieldwork report in multiple files and the most suitable formats makes it easily reusable for researchers.

If you want to ensure that your fieldwork report is prepared correctly and that the review process runs smoothly, contact us to discuss the best methodology for your research project at amcr@arup.cas.cz (support for Bohemia) or amcr@arub.cz (support for Moravia and Silesia).

amcrPas.hero.intro: Want to help advance scientific research and preserve our archaeological heritage?

amcrPas.about.label: About the project
amcrPas.about.title: About the AMCR-PAS
amcrPas.about.description: The Portal of Amateur Collaborators and the Register of Individual Finds (AMCR-PAS) is a joint initiative of the Institutes of Archaeology of the Czech Academy of Sciences in Prague and Brno to promote citizen science in archaeology. Its aim is to systematically record finds made by the amateur collaborators working with archaeological institutions.
amcrPas.about.description2: The AMCR-PAS is part of the Archaeological Map of the Czech Republic, and thus part of the Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic (AIS CR). It serves to register finds, manage collaborations, and share data with both the professional community and the general public.
amcrPas.usefulInfo.title: Useful Information
amcrPas.usefulInfo.item1.title: Getting started with the AMCR-PAS
amcrPas.usefulInfo.item1.intro: Interested in collaborating through the AMCR-PAS? Here is how to get started.
amcrPas.usefulInfo.item1.section1Text: If you wish to get involved, contact an authorised archaeological organisation in your region to discuss opportunities for collaboration. Once an agreement is reached, their archaeologists will guide you through the registration process and explain how to use the AMCR-PAS system. For basic information, you can also attend the online training sessions we offer.

amcrPas.usefulInfo.item1.section2Text:
If you would like to use the AMCR-PAS to manage your network of collaborators and survey projects, you will find these resources helpful:

• FAQ
amcrPas.usefulInfo.item1.section2Footer: You can browse finds recorded in the AMCR-PAS via the Digital Archive.
amcrPas.usefulInfo.item2.title: AMCR-PAS training
amcrPas.usefulInfo.item2.intro: The Institutes of Archaeology regularly hold online training sessions dedicated to the AMCR-PAS system. You can sign up using this registration form.
amcrPas.usefulInfo.item2.section1List:
1) An overview of the basic code of practice for detectorists working in the field, the methodology of collaboration and its legal framework.

2) How the AMCR-PAS works: How to navigate the system and use it effectively.
amcrPas.usefulInfo.item2.section1Footer: Each training session ends with a discussion based on participants' questions.
amcrPas.usefulInfo.item2.section2List:
• Primarily for members of the public interested in collaboration
• Heritage and archaeology professionals are also welcome
amcrPas.usefulInfo.item2.section2Footer: The date of the training is announced several weeks in advance, based on expressed interest (usually once every six months). Before the session, you will receive all information by email, including the link to join.
amcrPas.usefulInfo.item3.title: What is the AMCR-PAS for?
amcrPas.usefulInfo.item3.intro: It is a tool for legal, methodologically guided collaboration between archaeological organisations and the public within the framework of citizen science. Its aim is to promote the responsible involvement of the public in the discovery and protection of archaeological heritage – not to legitimise illegal activities.
amcrPas.usefulInfo.item3.section1Text: As the experts and methodological guarantors designated by law to carry out archaeological research, the Institutes of Archaeology have long sought to cultivate and formally integrate amateur fieldwork activities in the Czech Republic into a legal framework. Their goal is to identify and support people who wish to collaborate within the limits of the law – that is, in professionally supervised archaeological projects.
amcrPas.usefulInfo.item3.section2Title: What the AMCR-PAS is not aiming for
amcrPas.usefulInfo.item3.section2Text: The purpose of the AMCR-PAS is not to legitimise illegal activities (such as unauthorised metal detecting), but to provide a formal framework for legal collaboration and its results. Our aim is to protect information and finds from being lost, ensure that each find can be traced, and help identify individuals who deliberately damage archaeological heritage.
amcrPas.usefulInfo.item4.title: The role of the Institutes of Archaeology
amcrPas.usefulInfo.item4.intro: Within the AMCR-PAS system, the Institutes of Archaeology of the Czech Academy of Sciences provide:
amcrPas.usefulInfo.item4.list:
1) Methodological support for archaeological institutions engaged in, approached for, or seeking to establish such collaboration in practice.

2) Negotiations with public authorities to harmonise approaches to enforcing statutory rules and to ensure that these activities are overseen by the relevant bodies (Ministry of Culture, regional authorities, etc.).

3) Education and the creation of an informed public network (in close cooperation with other archaeological institutions) working under professional supervision – the only lawful way to conduct archaeological research under the current legislation.

4) Technical support for collaborations via the AMCR-PAS portal – a specialised module of the Archaeological Map of the Czech Republic (AMCR) system, used for recording archaeological fieldwork in the Czech Republic.

amcrPas.faq.sectionTitle: Frequently asked questions from the public
amcrPas.faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions
amcrPas.faq.q1: Why cannot I search on my own? And why should I collaborate with professional organisations?
amcrPas.faq.a1:
Archaeological research is not a leisure activity – it is a professional endeavour subject to strict rules. Only authorised organisations are permitted to carry it out, i.e. those holding a licence from the Ministry of Culture of the Czech Republic and a formal agreement with the Czech Academy of Sciences (see list of organisations). Conducting an archaeological fieldwork without authorisation is an offence under the law, punishable by a fine of up to CZK 4 million.

Archaeological research is not limited to traditional excavations – it also includes activities such as surface collections or metal detector surveys.

Archaeological finds are not private property; they are the property of the region, municipality, or state. Anyone who searches for and keeps such finds is breaking the law. Cooperating with an authorised organisation, i.e. acting in accordance with the law, is legal, meaningful, and beneficial for you, the academic community, and, most importantly, for the protection of the Czech Republic's archaeological heritage.

Archaeology is a scientific discipline that requires professional methods, not only in large-scale excavations but also in non-invasive to minimally invasive surveys. Archaeological finds come with an archaeological context – information about their origin, significance, purpose, or why they were deposited in a specific location. This information is irreplaceable. If lost or incomplete, a find might lose its scientific and historical value. Authorised organisations train their collaborators to handle finds correctly and provide clear guidance on where and under what conditions searches may take place.
amcrPas.faq.q2: What is the purpose of the AMCR-PAS? Is it compliant with the law?
amcrPas.faq.a2:
The Archaeological Map of the Czech Republic (AMCR) is a professional tool for collecting, managing, and archiving data obtained from archaeological fieldwork. The AMCR-PAS module was specifically designed to record data from metal detector surveys and surface collections carried out by authorised archaeological organisations and their official collaborators from the public (citizen or volunteer collaborators). The system's legality is unquestionable by its very nature.

The AMCR-PAS is primarily used for:
1) Recording finds, which are identified with the help of volunteer collaborators
2) Preserving essential information about a find's origin, location, and context
3) Standardising data collection within the field of archaeology

Its aim is to support responsible and professionally supervised collaboration between the public and authorised archaeological organisations.
amcrPas.faq.q3: Is it mandatory to use the AMCR-PAS? Why should I use it?
amcrPas.faq.a3:
Legal collaboration with archaeological institutions on metal detector surveys is only possible within the framework of current legislation, i.e. as part of authorised archaeological research, regardless of whether the AMCR-PAS system is used.

The AMCR-PAS is a tool designed to record data from surface collections and metal detector surveys. Its use benefits both parties.

For citizen collaborators:
• Quick and clear feedback on your own finds
• Viewing and tracking your finds at any time
• Access to a personal gallery of finds in the Digital Archive

For archaeological organisations:
• Digital communication with collaborators in one place
• Clear records of finds
• Easier data evaluation for scientific purposes

The basic requirement for public users of the AMCR-PAS is that they are legal collaborators of an organisation authorised to carry out archaeological fieldwork in the relevant area. Collaboration with archaeological institutions is possible without the AMCR-PAS, and many people already do so. Not all organisations fully use the AMCR-PAS module. However, this is gradually changing, and the use of the AMCR-PAS within authorised organisations is expected to become standard. Participation is always based on mutual agreement between the user and the organisation.
amcrPas.faq.q4: Which archaeological organisation should I collaborate with?
amcrPas.faq.a4:
Each authorised organisation has its own geographical area for conducting archaeological fieldwork. A full overview can be found on the Map of Archaeological Organisations. This is important as the collaboration with the public and the collection of archaeological finds are only possible within these designated areas. Therefore, it is a good idea to select and contact an organisation based on its geographical jurisdiction.

Keep in mind that not all institutions are able to support collaborators, whether due to their capacity, organisational structure, or specialisations. Not all authorised organisations focus on metal detector surveys, and not all can adequately manage portable finds long-term. Generally, museums, state or regional institutions, or the Institutes of Archaeology of the Czech Academy of Sciences tend to be more open to collaborating with the public. Your collaboration should be regular, long-term, and coordinated, so consider the accessibility of the organisation's headquarters from your home.
amcrPas.faq.q5: What if an organisation does not want to collaborate with me?
amcrPas.faq.a5:
As mentioned above, not all institutions have the same capacity or conditions for collaboration, which may also vary according to current workload. In such cases, you can contact another authorised organisation nearby. Almost every region has more than one organisation authorised to conduct archaeological fieldwork.

Successful and long-term collaboration requires mutual interest and an understanding of the relevant code of practice on the part of the public. Since many hobby detectorists operate illegally, it is essential to maintain mutual trust and a clear understanding that collaboration will be conducted in compliance with the law and will not threaten archaeological heritage. Citizen collaborators must follow all rules to ensure the continuation of this partnership.
amcrPas.faq.q6: What form should collaboration take? What should an agreement include?
amcrPas.faq.a6:
The partnership should primarily be based on a formal agreement. For the sake of transparency, a written agreement is strongly recommended. The agreement should include:

• Clear identification of the collaborator (the permit is non-transferable)

• The defined geographical and temporal scope of collaboration

• Institutional rules for donating finds and for communication between the archaeologist and the collaborator

• Contact details for both the collaborator and the archaeologist (phone number, email, etc.)

A sample agreement can be found here.
amcrPas.faq.q7: What does collaboration and fieldwork look like in practice?
amcrPas.faq.a7:
After signing the agreement, the citizen collaborator is trained in survey methods and handling of finds. These rules must be strictly followed. Training also covers the areas in which the collaborator may operate, the appropriate methods to apply, the use of the AMCR-PAS, and the basic photographic documentation of finds.

Before conducting a survey, the collaborator must inform the landowner of their intention and agree on conditions. Without at least verbal permission from the landowner, the survey cannot proceed.

All artefacts found must be handed over to the archaeologist from the relevant organisation, who will determine which items qualify as archaeological finds. Archaeological finds are not private property and belong by law to the region, municipality, or state. An organisation may only acquire a find from a collaborator if it has a concluded agreement with them.

If you encounter specific materials, such as firearms or ammunition produced after 1890, or human remains, stop the survey immediately and contact the responsible archaeologist. Firearms or ammunition must also be reported to the Czech Police immediately.
amcrPas.faq.q8: How do I prove that I am collaborating with an archaeological organisation?
amcrPas.faq.a8:
Collaborators must be able to provide confirmation of collaboration if requested by the landowner, the Czech Police, or other authorised persons. The permit must state the survey area, basic personal details (name, surname, year of birth), and its validity period. It must also include direct contact details for the responsible archaeologist. Ask the authorised organisation for information on how the permit is issued.

Keep in mind that this permit, together with an ID, is the only proof that you are acting legally at the site.
amcrPas.faq.q9: What should I pay attention to when recording a find in the AMCR-PAS?
amcrPas.faq.a9:
Instructions for recording finds can be found in the knowledge base. Ideally, entries should be made directly on site. Coordinates, registration number, and depth must always be recorded immediately (either in the AMCR-PAS or on another data medium). Additional information can be entered later, preferably after returning from the survey.

If you are participating in multiple projects, make sure to assign each find to the correct project. The responsible archaeologist approves the final record.
amcrPas.faq.q10: What happens to finds recorded in the AMCR-PAS?
amcrPas.faq.a10:
Data (especially finds) recorded in the AMCR-PAS are continuously published in the Digital Archive, where information is available to the academic community and, with certain restrictions, to the general public.

Finds made through metal detector surveys are an integral part of the Czech cultural heritage, and access to them is a fundamental human right (Articles 34 and 35 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights and Freedoms). The AMCR Digital Archive facilitates this. The extent of publicly available information is determined by the archaeologist responsible for the project. They may limit access to certain details, such as the exact findspot, to prevent potential illegal looting or damage to portable and non-portable archaeological heritage.
amcrPas.faq.q11: Am I entitled to a reward for my finds?
amcrPas.faq.a11:
Under Act No. 20/1987 Coll., on State Monument Care (as amended), a reward is only granted for chance finds (Section 23), i.e. accidental discoveries made during gardening or agricultural work. This does not apply to finds made as part of active searching, which constitutes archaeological research.

If the research is unauthorised (not conducted by an authorised organisation, or not approved and recorded in the AMCR), it is an offence under Section 39(2)(f) of the same Act. In such cases, a fine of up to CZK 4 million may be imposed, along with confiscation of equipment used in the offence (e.g. metal detector).

These provisions do not prevent authorised organisations from offering rewards or benefits to collaborating volunteers as recognition of their contribution. Such rewards are discretionary and fully under the authority of the relevant institution.
amcrPas.faq.sectionProfessional: Frequently asked questions from archaeological organisations
amcrPas.faq.q12: What is the purpose of the AMCR-PAS? Is it in compliance with current legislation?
amcrPas.faq.a12: Like other components of the AMCR, the AMCR-PAS is a tool for collecting, managing, and archiving archaeological data from metal detector surveys and surface collections (i.e. activities falling into the category of 'archaeological survey') carried out by authorised archaeological organisations and their officially approved collaborators from the public (known as citizen or volunteer collaborators). By its nature, the legality of the system is not in question. The AMCR-PAS serves as an instrument for the unified collection and storage of data originating from archaeological surveys (whether group-based or, in particular, individual) involving members of the public under the supervision and guarantee of professional archaeologists in accordance with applicable legal regulations.
amcrPas.faq.q13: Is the use of the AMCR-PAS mandatory?
amcrPas.faq.a13:
It is not the intention of the Institutes of Archaeology to force authorised organisations to collaborate with the public beyond their usual activities, established practice, or current needs. However, if an authorised organisation does collaborate with members of the public in a way that results in the acquisition of portable finds, it is obliged to keep a record of such finds, including all relevant and available metadata. Any fieldwork can still be managed through the standard AMCR procedure; the use of the AMCR-PAS system is voluntary. PAS, however, has been specifically designed for surveys conducted by individual collaborators whose work is officially approved and integrated into the research activities of each authorised organisation. It is therefore more practical for the administration of such surveys and facilitates the fulfilment of related obligations towards the Institutes of Archaeology of the Czech Academy of Sciences.

The AMCR-PAS offers features that enable the active involvement of collaborators in creating records, along with adjustable levels of data accessibility for the community of finders and the general public. This can also serve as an incentive to engage in searching within a legal framework and under professional supervision. The more widely the AMCR-PAS is used in archaeology, the greater its contribution will be to heritage preservation, scientific research, and archaeological outreach.

All obligations arising from legal regulations and agreements between the authorised organisation and the Czech Academy of Sciences apply regardless of the chosen recording method.
amcrPas.faq.q14: Does the AMCR-PAS serve to manage rescue or research excavations?
amcrPas.faq.a14: Following the launch of the AMCR-PAS, a new type of archaeological project was introduced – the survey. Unlike excavations triggered by construction or other intrusive activities, these surveys respond to the general and long-term threats posed to sites or larger areas by natural erosion, agricultural activity, or illegal looting. They rely on non-invasive or only minimally invasive methods. In essence, they represent a form of preventive rescue archaeology, aimed at protecting endangered portable finds that, in most cases, have already been removed from their original context. For projects in this category, there is no need to obtain a statement from the Institutes of Archaeology, as is required for scientific research involving trial trenches or large-scale excavations. Instead, a brief summary of the project's objectives must simply be submitted to the AMCR.
amcrPas.faq.q15: What are the key criteria for creating and managing individual projects?
amcrPas.faq.a15:
Survey-type projects should be established with a clearly defined spatial and chronological framework. Within this framework, projects are expected to be completed, accompanied by a fieldwork report, and submitted for archiving. In principle, the following workstreams can arise:

• Surface collection projects: These serve to record the results of surveys carried out in cooperation with the amateur public within a predefined territorial unit (e.g. district, list of municipalities in line with the geographical remit of the authorised organisation, individual cadastral areas). The maximum permissible area of such a project corresponds to the current administrative boundaries of a region. However, projects may also be created for individual districts, cadastral areas, or their combinations. In no case may a project extend beyond the geographical remit of the respective archaeological organisation.
• Other projects may be created, for instance, for targeted monitoring of a specific site or group of sites. In such cases, the requirement for closure after one year does not necessarily apply; however, the project must always have a clearly defined time frame stated in the documentation and should be concluded with a fieldwork report within several survey seasons (no later than five years).
• For retrospective entries or chance finds pursuant to Section 23(2–5) of the State Monument Care Act (No. 20/1987 Coll.), independent ad hoc projects may be created. The geographical limitations apply here in the same way as for surface collection projects.
• To record finds of uncertain origin (see the next question, second paragraph), an individual survey-type project should be created, covering the geographical remit of the authorised organisation.

Each project enables to record finds separately, which simplifies their management. When projects are logically structured, several projects may be created for the same period if needed. In case of uncertainty regarding the creation of projects, please contact the designated administrators of the AMCR-PAS system, who will be happy to advise you.

Further information can be found in the Manual for Archaeologists.
amcrPas.faq.q16: What types of finds can be managed in the AMCR-PAS? What should be recorded and how?
amcrPas.faq.a16:
The AMCR-PAS focuses on the collection and management of information on archaeological finds originating from official collaborations with responsible and trained members of the public. This partnership may take the form of organised surveys under direct professional supervision or individual, but officially approved and guided, prospecting activity within a registered project. Such projects can be defined in very general terms, covering a wide range of individual collaborators' activities, but always in line with the geographical remit of the authorised organisation as defined in its agreement with the Czech Academy of Sciences. The geographical scope and activities carried out within such a project may not exceed the territorial competence of the authorised organisation or any other legally binding limits on its powers.

The AMCR-PAS is not intended to manage artefacts clearly acquired through illegal activities. Its primary purpose is to record finds discovered by members of the public with a demonstrable connection to a specific authorised organisation.

Finds acquired by an authorised organisation but originating outside its geographical remit cannot be recorded by them. Instead, such finds must be passed on to the organisation authorised to carry out research in that area, and only that organisation may record them following a professional assessment.

In the case of a genuine chance find and compliance with Section 23(2–5) of the State Monument Care Act (No. 20/1987 Coll.), the find may be recorded in the AMCR-PAS.

Artefacts that have not been physically handed over to an authorised organisation (e.g. only shown) cannot be recorded in the AMCR-PAS.
amcrPas.faq.q17: The survey is subject to, among other things, an agreement with the landowner (or manager/user). How should authorised organisations approach this obligation when collaborating with members of the public?
amcrPas.faq.a17:
It is clearly impractical to secure such agreements in advance, especially in the case of collaborators with a large operational range who search for new sites. There are also many landowners, especially farmers, who will allow access but are unwilling to complete the required paperwork.

The Institutes of Archaeology currently recommend that agreements between a collaborator and an authorised organisation include a clause obliging the collaborator to comply fully with all relevant legislative provisions and authorising them to obtain permission to access land for activities they are permitted to perform. The collaborator bears full responsibility for any damage caused to third parties in the course of their activities (there is no requirement for the landowner's permission to be in written form).
amcrPas.faq.q18: How will the issue of maintaining two or three separate records of finds in collecting institutions be addressed?
amcrPas.faq.a18:
This risk can only be partially mitigated. Currently, only some museum system providers import the AMCR data. The AMCR tools, especially the AMCR API, can be used for integration into any information system; however, specific requirements must be submitted by system users to their providers. The Institutes of Archaeology offer the necessary methodological and technical support in this regard.

Unlike other databases, the AMCR-PAS is the only one fully accessible to the public, linked to map interfaces, and ensuring compliance with the State Monument Care Act. While processing a larger number of finds will inevitably increase the workload, records that meet the requirements of the State Monument Care Act must still be kept (processing records from detectorists in the form of standard fieldwork reports is also a considerable workload). The Institutes of Archaeology are making every effort to persuade the governing bodies of authorised organisations of the need to strengthen staffing capacity and to support the targeted implementation of the AMCR-PAS.

Accession numbers or other identifiers can be entered into the PAS as the inventory number in the 'Storage' section of the form.
amcrPas.faq.q19: Can archaeological finds be recorded in the AMCR-PAS retrospectively?
amcrPas.faq.a19: Yes, finds may be recorded retrospectively in the PAS. The record should be created by the authorised organisation managing the finds. For retrospective recording, it is important to create a new individual project or projects to avoid merging the records of new finds with older artefacts of different origin, and to ensure that each set is described consistently and to a high standard.
amcrPas.faq.q20: What form should collaboration between archaeological organisations and members of the public take? What should an agreement contain?
amcrPas.faq.a20:
The partnership should primarily be based on a formal agreement. For the sake of transparency, a written agreement is strongly recommended. The agreement should include:

• Clear identification of the collaborator (the permit is non-transferable)

• The defined geographical and temporal scope of collaboration

• Institutional rules for donating finds and for communication between the archaeologist and the collaborator

• Contact details for both the collaborator and the archaeologist (phone number, email, etc.)

A sample collaboration agreement can be found here.

A sample training protocol for collaborators can be found here.

If the authorised organisation has a different practice, the sample agreement can be replaced by other employment law instruments, such as an Agreement to Complete a Job or an Agreement to Perform Work. This approach is particularly suitable for experienced, long-term, and thoroughly vetted collaborators.
amcrPas.faq.q21: How should amateur collaborators identify themselves?
amcrPas.faq.a21:
A collaborator must be able to present confirmation of collaboration. This confirmation must clearly and easily indicate the area in which the person is authorised to carry out surveys, to whom it was issued (non-transferable), and the period of validity (one year, with the option of extension is recommended). It should also contain a direct and, if possible, permanently accessible contact for the issuing body, i.e. the archaeologist responsible for the survey. It is also recommended to include the collaborator's AMCR-PAS identification number, as this is unique and verifiable (e.g. U-001234).

Currently, there is no unified format for such a confirmation or permit card issued by authorised organisations. The only requirement is that it must contain all of the above information. Some organisations or regions may prefer their own solutions, including distinctive graphic designs. If there is interest, the Institutes of Archaeology are prepared to design and produce a unified card format for organisations or regions that request it.
